title: A morning word
hook: a line from a text you love
tomorrow: a man moves to a new city for love. does his journey count?

segments.voice: Yesterday, breath before phone: the Buddha teaching his elders to know each breath, long as long, short as short. Today the morning gets words.

Some people keep one quote on the lock screen for years. Others want a fresh verse of the day every morning. Desert monks wrestled with something close to this. John Cassian tells how he and his friend Germanus traveled to Egypt to learn from the desert elders, and asked one of them, Abba Isaac, a question they couldn't let go of: how do you pray without ceasing, when the mind won't sit still for a minute? His answer was a single line.
screen: `ONE QUOTE FOR YEARS, OR A NEW ONE DAILY?` → `TWO MONKS GO TO EGYPT.` → `HOW DO YOU PRAY ALWAYS?`

segments.voice: The line is from a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me." Isaac's case: say it on waking, at work, when you're tempted, when you're glad. One short verse fits every mood, so the mind always has a place to come home to. That's one view: one line, kept for life. The other view lives in the same monasteries. Benedict's Rule sets hours every day for lectio, slow reading, and the monk reads on, so the reading keeps moving through new pages. Let both speak. For the daily reading: a single line can wear smooth and go dead in the mouth, and a new page keeps surprising you. For the one verse: a new line every day can turn into browsing, and the one line goes deep because it never changes. The monasteries kept both. Benedict's monks open their hours of prayer with Isaac's very verse, and then they read on, page by page. Here is the teaching under it. In the Christian monastic tradition, a word of scripture is meant to be carried, not only read: repeated until it sinks in, so the day is lived inside it. On your own path the question is which you need right now: a line to come home to, or a line to wake you up.
screen: `ONE VERSE FOR EVERY MOOD.` · `OR LECTIO: READ ON, DAY BY DAY.` · `THE MONASTERIES KEPT BOTH.` · `A WORD CARRIED, NOT ONLY READ.` · then, large: `MY MORNING LINE.`

segments.voice: Choose a line you could carry: Isaac's verse, a line of a poem, a sentence from a text you love. Say it out loud, slowly, three times, and notice which word lands heaviest. If it still sounds true the third time, write it under tomorrow's first minute in your notebook.
A morning word: one line you carry into the day. For Abba Isaac, a single psalm verse; for Benedict's readers, the next page.
Keep this close: my morning line, a word carried, not only read. Back again tomorrow.

Abba Isaac.meaning: a desert elder in Egypt who taught Cassian how to pray

John Cassian.meaning: a monk who wrote down the desert elders' teaching

Germanus.meaning: Cassian's friend and fellow traveler in the desert

lectio.meaning: Latin for reading: the monks' slow, prayerful reading of scripture

Benedict's Rule.meaning: Benedict of Nursia's short rule for monastic life
